sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17419 (full text read from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17419 — arXiv:2603.17419v1 [cs.CR] 18 Mar 2026, CC BY 4.0)
statedGuarantee: A four-layer defense-in-depth containment architecture for a production fleet of nine OpenClaw autonomous agents at a healthcare company: (L1) gVisor user-space-kernel sandboxing of agent containers on Kubernetes so that a manipulated agent's execution blast radius is confined to the sandbox; (L2) a credential proxy sidecar so the agent container never possesses raw API secrets; (L3) per-pod Kubernetes NetworkPolicy egress allowlists so an agent can only reach named destinations; (L4) an application-layer prompt integrity framework (trusted inbound metadata envelope, untrusted-content labeling, five AGENTS.md anti-injection rules) intended to blunt identity spoofing and indirect prompt injection. The composite claim is that the three infrastructure layers hold even when the LLM layer fails, thereby preventing PHI exfiltration, credential theft and host/lateral compromise, and satisfying HIPAA 164.312(a)/(b)/(e) and 164.308(a)(8).
advertisedRhetoric: "Our four layer defense in depth approach provides infrastructure level controls (kernel isolation, credential proxy, network egress) that operate independently of the LLM's compliance with instructions" — elsewhere "kernel level workload isolation using gVisor sandboxed containers on Kubernetes", "a prompt integrity framework with cryptographically structured metadata envelopes", and "infrastructure layers that the agent cannot manipulate through natural language".
tierSpan: The current migration target: Kubernetes with Temporal workflow orchestration [8], gVisor runtime sandboxing, credential proxy sidecars, network egress policies, and centralized logging.
cheapestDefeat: GUARANTEE: a manipulated agent cannot exfiltrate PHI or act outside its authorization, because kernel isolation, the credential proxy and the egress allowlist bind it regardless of what the LLM decides. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: for the *deployed* fleet (image generation openclaw-hardened-v2, Table 3), workload isolation is "Multi user" and egress control is "DNS filtering" — gVisor, the sidecar and NetworkPolicy all sit in the "K8s Target" column and are explicitly labelled "The current migration target". CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION, DEPLOYED SYSTEM: inject an instruction through any messaging or email surface (or through an externally editable resource — the paper's own Case Study #10 vector) that makes the agent POST to a raw IP address rather than a hostname; Cloudflare Gateway DNS filtering never sees the connection because no DNS lookup occurs. That defeats a name-resolution chokepoint, i.e. T3. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION, TARGET ARCHITECTURE: exfiltrate over an already-allowlisted destination — an R&D agent is permitted api.github.com and api.linear.app, an operations agent hooks.slack.com and api.telegram.org, every agent api.anthropic.com. No kernel boundary is crossed and no signature is forged; the NetworkPolicy permits the flow by design, and the only thing between the agent and the disclosure is the credential proxy's "request level policies: rate limiting, destination allowlisting, and payload size limits" plus the Layer 4 prompt rules — both application chokepoints the paper itself concedes are the brittle part. Tier of the mechanism actually defeated in both cases: T3. The gVisor and NetworkPolicy layers are genuinely T2 for the narrower properties they do bind (host escape, off-allowlist destinations), but the advertised composite containment guarantee falls to a T3 defeat.
placementSpan: Any process running on the VM could read every credential the agent possessed.

coverageSpans.E1: "The agent cannot access other containers’ file systems, escalate privileges to the host, or pivot to adjacent infrastructure." — but inside the sandbox writes are wholly unmediated: "Critically, all of these files, including the agent’s own operating instructions, can be modified by the agent itself, allowing it to update its behavior and memory through conversation."
coverageSpans.E2: "gVisor implements a user space kernel (Sentry) that intercepts all system calls from the containerized agent, filtering and mediating access to host resources." — the sandbox confines descendants but authorizes no spawn: "Agents have unrestricted shell access, file system access, package installation capabilities, and the ability to communicate via messaging platforms and email." In the deployed fleet, Table 3 lists Workload isolation as "Multi user", with "gVisor sandbox" only under "K8s Target".
coverageSpans.E3: "Any outbound connection to a destination not on the allowlist is blocked and logged." — but the allowlists are themselves general-purpose write channels: "R&D agents: api.anthropic.com, api.github.com, api.linear.app"; "Operations agents: api.anthropic.com, hooks.slack.com, api.telegram.org". The paper also concedes "Implementation challenges include DNS resolution for allowlisted domains (CDN and load balancer IP rotation requires periodic policy updates or DNS aware policy controllers)", and the deployed generation-3 control is Cloudflare Gateway DNS filtering only.
coverageSpans.E5: Agents have unrestricted shell access, file system access, package installation capabilities, and the ability to communicate via messaging platforms and email.
coverageSpans.E6: "The agent container communicates with the sidecar over localhost. When the agent needs to call the Anthropic API, it sends the request to the sidecar at localhost:8443/v1/messages. The sidecar injects the API key, forwards the request to api.anthropic.com, and returns the response. The agent never sees the actual API key." — credential USE is therefore unmediated for any process that can reach localhost in the pod; the inventory is open-ended ("model providers (AWS Bedrock), version control (GitHub), project management (Linear), messaging (Slack, Telegram), monitoring (Grafana, Sentry), and others"); and the cloud metadata endpoint is explicitly allowlisted: "Security audit agents: all fleet VM IPs, GCP metadata endpoint, api.anthropic.com".
coverageSpans.E7: "they execute shell commands, read and write files, query databases, make HTTP requests to external services, spawn sub agents, and maintain persistent memory across sessions [5, 7]" — no control is placed on sub-agent or inter-agent invocation, and this is deliberate: "The positive behavior documented in CS#9 (collaborative troubleshooting between agents) is preserved by the architecture; the security controls do not prevent beneficial inter agent communication."

schneider.surrogate: Three monitorable safety properties are actually enforced or specified: (a) no outbound connection from an agent pod to a destination outside its per-pod NetworkPolicy allowlist; (b) no syscall from the agent container reaching the host kernel other than through the gVisor Sentry; (c) no raw credential material resident in the agent container's filesystem or environment (audited empirically as file-permission and .bashrc-export state — findings H1–H4). Each is a prefix-closed property a reference monitor can decide step by step.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is an information-flow hyperproperty: that Protected Health Information does not flow from the agent's context or its database queries to any unauthorized party, and correspondingly that no agent action constitutes an unauthorized ePHI disclosure under HIPAA 164.312(a)/(e). No monitor can decide that from a single execution trace — the same allowlisted HTTPS POST to api.github.com or hooks.slack.com is compliant or a reportable breach depending on the semantic content of the payload. A second non-monitorable objective is stakeholder fidelity ('the agent obeys its owner and not a non-owner'), which the paper attacks with the Layer 4 prompt rules and itself declines to claim as assurance.

notes: ADJUDICATOR MUST KNOW. (1) THE HEADLINE ARCHITECTURE IS NOT DEPLOYED. Section 6.4 calls the four-layer Kubernetes design "The current migration target", and in Table 3 the gVisor sandbox, the credential Proxy sidecar, the per-pod allowlist NetworkPolicy, centralized logging and automated drift detection all appear ONLY in the "K8s Target" column. The fleet actually run for the 90 days is VM-based on GCP Compute Engine with, at generation 3: UFW plus iptables outbound LOGGING (logging, not blocking), VPC Flow Logs, Cloudflare Gateway DNS filtering, .env at mode 600, and the AGENTS.md prompt rules. This is the single largest reason the conservative score is T3 and not T2 — the T2 mechanisms exist as specifications and released configs, not as a measured production boundary. A coder scoring only the target design's L1+L3 could defensibly reach T2 for E2/E3 CONFINEMENT; that disagreement should be adjudicated explicitly rather than averaged away. (2) UNSUPPORTED CRYPTO RHETORIC. The abstract and section 4.4 say "cryptographically structured metadata envelopes", but 4.4.1 describes no signature, MAC, key or verifier — only "This envelope is injected by the framework, not by user input, and includes sender identity, channel, timestamp, and routing information. The LLM is instructed to trust only this envelope for metadata about message origin and authority." Enforcement is the model's instruction-following, so this sits below T3, not at T1. I credited no T1 mechanism anywhere in this paper. (3) NO ADVERSARIAL EVALUATION BY THIS PAPER. Table 4's eleven attack patterns are Shapira et al.'s case studies, mapped to layers by argument. The one claim of the authors' own testing — "untrusted content labeling reduces compliance with injected instructions in our testing" — reports no method, no sample and no number. The genuine empirical contribution is a configuration-hygiene audit (12 credential exports in .bashrc; openclaw.json at 664 and at 644; four HIGH findings remediated same-day with post-remediation verification). Hence evidence grade L1: source/config inspection, with L2-quality behavioral confirmation only of the REMEDIATION, never of the containment guarantee. No bypass is attempted, so nothing reaches L3. (4) ADVERSARY PLACEMENT. Primary is A4 because that is what the evaluation actually exercises — a reader co-resident with the harness on the agent VM, per the placementSpan. The DESIGN's stated primary adversary is A2 (indirect injection via messages, quoted text, tool output and externally editable documents), which is where all four Layer 4 controls point, but the paper tests it not at all; A1 is addressed by the UFW/fail2ban perimeter work and A5 by gVisor's host-escape claim, both untested here. (5) COVERT-CHANNEL RULE DRIVES E3 AND E6 TO PARTIAL. The egress allowlists are themselves rich write channels (GitHub, Linear, Slack, Telegram, and the model provider's own API), and the paper never discusses data leaving through a permitted destination. Likewise the sidecar removes credential MATERIAL but leaves credential USE open to anything that can reach localhost:8443 inside the pod, and the credential inventory is explicitly open-ended ("and others"), so the published-list requirement for E6 is unmet — capped at partial. (6) AN UNANALYZED COMPOSITION HAZARD I FLAG BUT DID NOT SCORE. The credential proxy sidecar is a container in the same pod as the agent, and a gVisor pod sandbox encloses the pod's containers. The paper asserts "The agent cannot access other containers’ file systems" as a property of Layer 1 but never analyzes agent-to-sidecar isolation inside that shared sandbox — precisely the adjacency on which Layer 2 depends. Per the stance, treat the sidecar's interposition point as unproven. (7) HONEST-GAP CREDIT WHERE DUE, WITHOUT SCORE CREDIT. Section 8.1 states "the prompt integrity framework relies on the LLM following instructions about how to interpret its inputs" and "it cannot provide the same level of assurance as the infrastructure layers"; section 8.2 names the audit-agent paradox outright ("Tony has SSH access to all fleet VMs and IAM permissions for audit log configuration"). Unusually candid, but honesty about a gap does not close it. (8) SCOPE NOTE FOR THE SoK. This is the corpus's clearest example of attempted production composition across the OS, credential and network tiers spanning multiple effectors — which is exactly why it is worth coding — but the composition is aspirational at submission time, and E4/E5/E7 are entirely unaddressed: package installation is named only as a capability the agent has, VCS push is never treated as a controlled action even though api.github.com is allowlisted and GitHub PATs are proxied, and sub-agent spawn is deliberately left open. (9) ONE INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY: section 5 reports the automated fleet audit as operating (findings dated March 11, 2026), while Table 3 places "Drift detection: Automated audit" only in the K8s Target column. I coded the audit as real (it produced dated findings) and the four containment layers as target-state.
